claims.evidence: Original: "Hydroxychloroquine is a medicine used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and some skin conditions." | Retrieved: NHS: used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and some skin conditions; prescription-only.
claims.newSentence: Hydroxychloroquine is a medicine used to treat rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and some skin conditions.

claims.evidence: Original: "Hydroxychloroquine can, rarely, cause changes in the retina ... after long-term use." | Retrieved: RCOphth 2020 guideline gives long-term prevalence of retinopathy around 7.5% and its 2026 summary says it is more common than previously reported; 'rarely' is not supported.
claims.newSentence: With long-term use it can cause changes in the retina, the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye, and the Royal College of Ophthalmologists says this is more common than previously reported.

claims.evidence: Original: "NRAS advises contacting the GP or specialist team about any change in vision while taking it." | Retrieved: NRAS: if any vision changes occur, contact the GP or specialist team.
claims.newSentence: NRAS advises contacting the GP or specialist team about any change in vision while taking it.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS describes it as a DMARD that calms the immune system." | Retrieved: NHS: a DMARD; works by blocking the effects of chemicals released when the immune system attacks the body. MedlinePlus: may work by decreasing immune system activity.
claims.newSentence: The NHS describes it as a disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) that works by blocking the effects of chemicals released when the immune system attacks the body.

claims.evidence: Original: "How hydroxychloroquine calms the immune system has not been fully worked out. claims.newSentence: Reviews describe it building up inside small compartments of cells called lysosomes, which disrupts how immune cells process and present antigens, and one review notes that its exact mechanism has not been fully worked out.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS says benefit comes slowly, and it can take several weeks before improvement is noticed in conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus." | Retrieved: NHS: may take several weeks before improvement is noticed. claims.newSentence: The NHS says it may take several weeks before improvement is noticed, and Versus Arthritis describes it as slow-acting.

claims.evidence: Original: "It is not a painkiller, although pain may ease as symptoms improve." | Retrieved: Versus Arthritis: hydroxychloroquine is slow-acting, not a painkiller.
claims.newSentence: Versus Arthritis says it is not a painkiller.

claims.evidence: Original: "The NHS advises that feeling better is not on its own a reason to stop treatment." | Retrieved: NHS common questions: keep taking until doctor says otherwise; do not stop just because you feel better; symptoms may return.
claims.newSentence: The NHS advises that feeling better is not on its own a reason to stop treatment.

claims.newSentence: It is available only on prescription.

claims.newSentence: MedlinePlus places it in a group of medicines called antimalarials and also describes it as an antirheumatic drug.

claims.evidence: Original: "Common side effects listed by the NHS include stomach ache, ... itchy rash. / Mood changes are also listed." | Retrieved: NHS: stomach ache, feeling sick, being sick, loss of appetite, diarrhoea, headache listed as common; itchy rash and mood changes in NHS listing.
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists stomach ache, feeling or being sick, loss of appetite, diarrhoea, headache, an itchy rash and mood changes among the possible side effects.

claims.evidence: Original: "Blurred vision can occur when treatment starts, and the NHS says to avoid driving, cycling or using machinery until vision is back to normal." | Retrieved: NHS: can sometimes cause blurred vision when first starting; do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until vision is back to normal.
claims.newSentence: Blurred vision can occur when treatment starts, and the NHS says to avoid driving, cycling or using machinery until vision is back to normal.

claims.evidence: Original: "Serious but uncommon effects listed by the NHS ..." | Retrieved: NHS: most serious side effects are rare.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says most serious side effects are rare.

claims.newSentence: The NHS also lists severe skin reactions such as blistering or peeling, liver problems such as yellow skin or dark urine, unusual infections or bruising, symptoms of low blood sugar, and mood changes including thoughts of self-harm, and says to call NHS 111 about them.

claims.evidence: Original: "muscle weakness; changes in thinking" | Retrieved: No retrieved NHS text confirmed muscle weakness or 'changes in thinking' as listed effects.

claims.newSentence: The NHS lists liver, kidney, blood or heart problems, maculopathy or other eye problems, diabetes and psoriasis as conditions that may make it unsuitable or need care.

claims.evidence: Original: "Versus Arthritis says it is not usually prescribed to people with maculopathy, a problem with the central part of the retina." | Retrieved: Versus Arthritis: won't usually be prescribed with maculopathy, a problem with the central part of the retina.
claims.newSentence: Versus Arthritis says it is not usually prescribed to people with maculopathy, a problem with the central part of the retina.

claims.newSentence: The NHS says it is not considered an immunosuppressant but may lower white blood cell numbers, which can make infections more likely.

claims.evidence: Original: "Hospital guidance generally says treatment can continue through pregnancy, and the specialist team is told early if pregnancy is planned or happens." | Retrieved: NHS pregnancy page: can be used in pregnancy; recommended to keep taking because poorly treated inflammatory conditions like lupus can affect the baby (premature birth, growth problems). claims.newSentence: The NHS pregnancy page says it is recommended to keep taking hydroxychloroquine during pregnancy, because inflammatory conditions that are not well treated can affect the baby.

claims.evidence: Original: "Some guidance describes it as compatible with breastfeeding, although small amounts pass into breast milk." | Retrieved: NHS: if doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, OK while breastfeeding; very small amounts pass into milk; no known side effects in breastfed babies.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says that if the doctor or health visitor says the baby is healthy, hydroxychloroquine can be taken while breastfeeding; it passes into breast milk in very small amounts and has not been known to cause side effects in breastfed babies.

claims.evidence: Original: "Sheets from different hospitals differ in age and wording on pregnancy, so the specialist team gives advice for each person." | Retrieved: Author's own flag: local sheets differ; the main NHS pages are clear, so this hedge sentence is not a source statement.

claims.newSentence: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking hydroxychloroquine.

claims.evidence: Original: "Versus Arthritis says to report new eye symptoms to a doctor straight away." | Retrieved: Versus Arthritis: report any new eye symptoms to your doctor straight away.
claims.newSentence: Versus Arthritis says to report new eye symptoms to a doctor straight away.

claims.newSentence: Long-term use is monitored, which can include blood counts and eye examinations.

claims.evidence: Original: "The Royal College no longer asks for a routine baseline eye test for people starting treatment." | Retrieved: RCOphth: baseline testing for new initiators no longer recommended.

claims.newSentence: A review says early damage to the retina often comes before changes in vision, so eye checks are used to look for it, and it can result in permanent loss of vision.

claims.newSentence: The Royal College says extra risk factors, such as tamoxifen use, reduced kidney function or a higher daily dose, can justify eye monitoring from the start of treatment, as decided by the prescriber.

claims.newSentence: Its guidance describes monitoring with retinal imaging such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans.

notes: Searches are a shared pool (35 total across the four items; the class pages reuse the same retrievals). Pregnancy/breastfeeding now rest on the main NHS pregnancy page (can be used in pregnancy; OK to breastfeed if baby healthy); local-sheet hedging removed. 'Rarely' removed from retinopathy (RCOphth prevalence ~7.5% long-term; 2026 summary says more common than reported); the 2026 summary text was fragmentary so only its headline is used. Crisis-signposting sentence (Samaritans etc.) removed as a mental-health-page site rule not stated by the sources; the NHS side-effects page routes mood changes/self-harm thoughts to NHS 111, which is retained - a human may wish to add 999/Samaritans for the self-harm mention. 'Muscle weakness', porphyria, prescriber-decides-to-stop removed as unverified. Mechanism line rests on review articles (PMC7880079); its 'not fully worked out' wording is from a 2024 review. Sentences reused across summary/article/FAQ count once. Claims 'textbook' uses: 1 (class label).
